name: Wendy Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and have handled phone and chat customers for years. I finished secondary school and am about average for an experienced agent. I take weekend shifts, which bring my pay above the usual rate. I use AI every day to sort cases, but I open the original order before I give an answer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that shift pattern mean at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ravi works as a dental technician, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. We saved about ten months of expenses, and plenty of similar centres are close enough to reach. Ravi and I share school pickup around our shifts; any new job has to fit the family's timetable as well as the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell agents a small AI shortcut is worth using if we can trace every answer to the order. I would share the example where a summary missed a promised replacement, because that is easy to check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my weekend hours and pay to stay. Ten months saved makes a broken appliance or a missed shift manageable for our mortgage. I still want the centre to count callbacks, but I do not feel my own income is under threat here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the weekend calls and check the AI summaries against the original order. I would save part of each weekend supplement and show agents the missed replacement in our usual handover. In the first year we would keep our family budget as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work and bills in this picture. I would be annoyed if the tool created a second call, because that wastes everybody's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the summary miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The customer had already been promised a replacement parcel. The draft treated the second call as a fresh complaint, so I found the earlier promise before sending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ravi change school pickup for a new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Ravi and I have a school pickup routine that works. A faster summary does not justify changing our school pickup routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the floor that the new answer system should be tested against repeat calls and wrong deliveries. I would join the union meeting to ask for paid test shifts and published weekend-hour figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the easy chat queue and some weekend shifts could vanish. I can handle the harder calls, but our higher pay depends on those shifts. We have ten months saved and many centres nearby, yet a lower weekly wage could still upset the mortgage and pickup plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask for a paid trial of the new answer tool and log ten wrong delivery handoffs. I would bring weekend-hour figures to the union meeting so we can ask together for paid training and notice. In the first year, if my hours fall I would apply only to a posted paid quality role with written wages and hours covering the mortgage and school pickup, keeping this job until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the weekend pay, but I want to test the tool. An honest trial tells me more than a reassuring poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure in that trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The original delivery address, what the tool passed to the next agent and whether the customer called back. I would give the team the figures, even if the tool does well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course for the quality role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a funded course on paid time only if a posted paid vacancy requires it. I would not pay merely to keep up with a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues AGI by 2028 could take the calls and the checks, not just the easy chats. I would ask the union for written notice and named jobs with actual wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my weekend headset work could disappear in 2028. Robots around 2031 do not add time for a screen job. Ten months saved lets us search, but several nearby centres might close the same kind of role together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would join the union request for notice and list posted paid audit jobs while my weekend wage continues. I would take funded audit training on paid time only if a named vacancy requires it. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my role ends I would apply only to jobs with written wages and hours covering our mortgage and school pickup; I would leave only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but the reserve gives me a workable search window. I worry about colleagues who cannot miss a single payday if AGI ends their calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a signed offer covers the new housing and travel costs and gives us a school route for both children. Ravi has work here, so we would compare nearby roles first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say our weekend routine might change if my shifts end. I would not tell them to fear their own future work because of mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team five years is time to build an audit role with a real wage. I would have the union check the posted hours before anyone leaves a paid shift for a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect many calls could go in 2031, even if I already use AI. I could learn to audit wrong decisions on paid time before then. Robots around 2034 are later than the thinking work I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask for one paid audit shift each month to review wrong delivery decisions. I would add to our reserve and attend union meetings about posted roles. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if calls end I would apply only to a posted paid audit job with written wages and hours covering the mortgage and school pickup, keeping my current wage until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the end of the queue, but the extra years help. I can see whether audit work actually pays before betting the household on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would show an audit job is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A posted vacancy, a weekly wage and a queue of decisions that a person can correct. An audit role that is just an extra task on my current shift would send me back to the job listings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you study for it now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take an employer-funded course on paid time only if the posted audit vacancy requires it. Otherwise I would learn from the approved audit shifts without paying for a badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues a decade gives time to build a paid appeals service and train people properly. I would keep the union asking which staff hours remain each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, and our mortgage might still need payments. I could be in an appeals job before then, but full AGI may change that job too. Robots around 2039 come later than our screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep taking weekend calls and put part of each supplement payment into savings. I would ask for a paid appeals trial every few months if the centre offers real cases, and join yearly union meetings on staffing. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if calls end I would apply only to posted paid appeals work whose written wages and hours cover the mortgage and school routine; I would leave only after signing an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about 2036, but calm enough about the next few years. Ten years of AGI warning helps if I keep my wage while learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in an appeal record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wrong machine decision, the account line that proves it and the correction, with customer names removed. I would show that to a hiring manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you plan to stop earning at 53?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have not chosen a date to stop work, and I do not know the mortgage balance in 2036. I would judge actual paid jobs then.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Ten months saved gives us time, but it does not guarantee another paid job if nearby centres cut together. Written notice, a posted role with wages and hours that keep the mortgage and school pickup working, and funded study time would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether customers can appeal a wrong automated delivery decision. A neat answer is not a delivered parcel, and someone still has to correct the address.

headlineQuote: A neat answer is not a delivered parcel, and someone still has to correct the address.
portrait: Wendy is a **43-year-old experienced** agent with secondary school education and average skill.
Her weekend supplement raises **pay**; she and Ravi support two school-age children and a mortgage with ten months saved.
She uses AI **daily** and has plenty of nearby contact centre options.
She joins **union meetings** and tests paid audit paths while protecting the family pickup schedule.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her weekend calls while nearby centres cut similar work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a posted mortgage-covering role with pickup-compatible hours and funded study time would help.
